title: Set a gym weight stack to 70 lb: pull the selector pin and push it fully home in the 70-lb plate
instruction: Set the weight stack to 70 lb.
context: Moving the pin on a weight stack is the first thing anyone does at a cable machine or a home gym, and everyone who has been to a gym has watched it done. The pin (9.5 mm, 3/8 in) must come out of the old plate against its magnet and go fully home through the chosen plate into the selector stem's cross hole, which sits hidden 6 cm inside the plate and is only 0.5 mm wider all round than the pin. The hand has to bring the pin level and square to the 13 mm bore at the right plate (plates are 2.5 cm apart) and keep it straight while it pushes 11.5 cm in, letting the rounded tip find the hidden hole; a tilted pin catches on the stem, and a pin left half in lifts only the top plate. Manuals insist on it: "Make sure that the weight pin is inserted fully into the weight stack before you exercise" (Gold's Gym GGSY30580); "Be certain that weight pins are completely inserted prior to exercising" (Nautilus NS200). One arm does it, as a person does.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. (1) Base, fixed: steel frame foot 19 x 34 x 5.25 cm, x 30.5 to 49.5, y -20 to 14; two 1-inch chrome guide rods rise from it at x 40, y -13.5 and 7.5, to a top bar 52-54 cm up. (2) Weight stack: twelve black steel 10-lb plates, 28 cm wide (y) x 15 cm deep (x) x 2.5 cm thick, weights printed in white on their fronts (10 to 120 lb, top down); fronts at x 32.5, y -17 to 11, stacked from 5.3 to 35.6 cm up. Each has a 3 cm square middle hole and a 13 mm square bore from the middle of its front face (y -3) across the middle hole to 2.5 cm short of its back. Plates 2-12 ride on the rods, free to rise; the top plate is fixed to the stem. The 70-lb plate's middle is 19.2 cm up, the 40-lb plate's 26.8 cm. (3) Selector stem: 2.5 cm square steel bar at x 40, y -3, through every plate's middle hole to 41.6 cm, with a 10.5 mm square cross hole (along x) at the middle of each plate; cable on top. (4) Selector pin, loose, 0.11 kg: 9.5 mm (3/8 in) steel shaft 11.5 cm long from the knob's face to its rounded tip, red plastic knob 4.4 cm across, 2.5 cm long, with a magnet (holds until pulled with 6 N). It starts fully home in the 40-lb plate (4th from the top): knob against the plate's face at x 32.5, y -3, 26.8 cm up. Both arms start at the ready pose, grippers open. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Every control step the scorer reads the pin's pose, each plate's height and each finger's collision-hull points. Lift test (the cable pulling the stem, as a person tugs the handle): once the pin has been touched and then left alone (no finger within 10 mm) for 1 s, the stem rises 4 cm at 1 cm/s, holds 0.5 s and comes back down; plates that rose 2 cm or more are counted (the top plate counts as one). It runs again after every new touch (a finger within 4 mm of the pin), which cancels the earlier result. 1.0 (success, held 1 s): the latest test, with the pin untouched since, raised exactly 7 plates (70 lb) and the pin is fully home (knob's face within 5 mm of the plate's face). 0.5: 7 plates raised but the pin not fully home (it carries the stack on its tip). 0: the latest test raised 2-6 or 8-12 plates (a wrong weight), or the pin was never drawn out of the 40-lb plate (doing nothing scores 0). 0.3: otherwise, if the pin was drawn fully out of the 40-lb plate (tip in front of the plates' faces) at some point: old setting cleared, no weight selected (a test raised only the top plate, the pin was still held at the end, or no test ran). Real trial, at the end of the run: if a gripper still holds the pin, no test; otherwise a person pulls the handle (or lifts the stem) about 4 cm and counts the plates that rise, and checks with a ruler that the knob is within 5 mm of the plate; the pull-out is seen on the video.
reset_notes: Lower the stack fully, pull the pin out wherever it is and push it fully home in the 40-lb plate (the 4th from the top), knob against the plate. Simulation: each trial starts the simulator afresh.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at true size, 20 Hz control. The pin's magnet is a joint that lets go for good at 6 N (estimate) and does not grip again. Plates weigh 1.0 kg in the sim, not 4.5 kg: with 4.5 kg the light pin was pushed through the bore wall during the lift test; the robot never moves the plates. The stem is stepped up 0.5 mm per control step, not pulled by a cable. The machine's frame, pulleys, handle and the pin's lanyard are left out.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both arms moved about near their bases and never reached the stack; the pin stayed in the 40-lb plate); demo: 1.0
